This is VinePair’s Booze News Weekly Roundup, where we gather the hottest headlines and product releases every Friday for a snapshot of what’s happening in the beverage alcohol industry. It was yet another quiet week on the Booze News front, but we have updates on write-downs at Treasury Wine Estates, Beyoncé bagging full ownership of SirDavis, the latest product releases, and more.

News to know:

  • Treasury Wine Estates takes impairments to U.S. business: The Australian wine producer, also the seventh-largest wine supplier in the United States, reduced the value of its American wine business with $395 million in write-downs, according to its fiscal year 2026 report. The new impairments mark the second time in nine months that Treasury has taken a ding to its U.S. assets, and the moves could point to Treasury’s intentions to pull out of the U.S. entirely.
  • A potential win for hemp-based beverages: With a potential de facto ban on THC products on the horizon, two members of the U.S. House of Representatives introduced a bipartisan bill on Monday that would establish guardrails for legally and safely producing and selling hemp-based beverages. The proposal came the same day that the Senate voted to postpone the federal ban on THC-based products until December.
  • Queen B of SirDavis Whisky: Beyoncé Knowles-Carter secured total ownership of SirDavis Rye Whisky after buying out LVMH’s stake in the brand. Beyoncé and LVMH debuted SirDavis together in 2024, marking the singer’s first foray into the spirits business.

Product releases to watch:

  • Brugal completes the Colección Visionaria series with a coconut-flavored rum: The luxury rum brand released Colección Visionaria Edición 03, Coconut, the final iteration of its three-year-long collection of ultra-premium Dominican rums. The rum is available at select retailers nationwide for a suggested retail price of $69.99.
  • $11,000 tequila from 1800: Proximo Spirits-owned 1800 Tequila is expanding its Colección Tequila lineup with a limited-edition extra añejo housed in a nickel decanter. The brand is only releasing 50 bottles of the tequila, titled Mono Laberinto Doble — available on the company’s site for a whopping $11,000.
  • Clase Azul raises funds for breast cancer awareness with new tequila: Clase Azul, known for its ornately decorated decanters, is releasing this year’s expression of its Pink Edición Limitada, a tequila packaged in a light pink bottle with a portion of its revenue going toward an organization promoting breast cancer awareness. Clase Azul Tequila Pink Edición Limitada 2026 is available in limited quantities at just six accounts worldwide for a suggested retail price of $1,400, and prices for previous years’ editions can go for over $3,000.

title: 7 Things You Should Know About Rolling Rock, the American Beer With a Mysterious Code on Every Bottle
summary:
When considering the name “Rolling Rock,” beer fans might associate the brand with hair-flipping, guitar-smashing rock and roll. content:
When considering the name “Rolling Rock,” beer fans might associate the brand with hair-flipping, guitar-smashing rock and roll. But the music genre didn’t emerge until the 1950s, and the story of Rolling Rock begins much earlier.

Rolling Rock was first produced at the Latrobe Brewing Company — a brewery founded in 1839 in Latrobe, Penn. At first, the brewery produced two labels, Latrobe Old German and Latrobe Pilsner, until a quintet of brothers took over and debuted Rolling Rock in 1939.

The extra pale lager has joined the ranks of America’s most iconic beer labels. Rolling Rock is perhaps most known for its signature green glass bottles and the number “33” embossed onto each bottle. (More on that later.) From that mysterious code to the brand’s contemporary branding, here are seven things to know about Rolling Rock.

  1. The Tito family bought the brewery that first produced Rolling Rock during Prohibition.

    The Latrobe Brewing Company’s facility went up for sale upon the onset of the 18th Amendment, and while many saw Prohibition as the end of America’s alcohol industry, five brothers of the Tito family took a chance on the return of the booze business in America. In 1932, when Prohibition was still in place, the brothers purchased Latrobe Brewing Company, and upon repeal in 1933, re-started production of the brewery’s old labels. Six years later, they decided to launch their own beer: Rolling Rock. In the decades that followed, the company underwent a number of changes in ownership, finally landing in the hands of Anheuser-Busch. The macro-brewing giant picked up the brand in 2006 before becoming Anheuser-Busch InBev in 2008.

  2. No one knows what the mysterious code means.

    The meaning behind the “33” on each bottle of Rolling Rock remains ambiguous: Even the brand’s website says, “Nobody knows.” However, that mystery has spurred a number of theories of what “33” could refer to. Some believe it’s a nod to the 33 steps involved in making beer, others purport it alludes to Rolling Rock’s brewing temperature, 33 degrees Fahrenheit. Additional theories suggest it hints at the year Prohibition was repealed, the number of stairs at the original brewery, among others.

  3. Rolling Rock once used an atypical brewing vessel…

    Since its debut Rolling Rock historically brewed and stored its beers in glass-lined tanks — unusual vessels for beermaking. Whereas most brewers use stainless steel unitanks for brewing, the original tanks insulated with glass helped reinforce the pale lager’s crisp, clean profile. Anheuser-Busch mostly ended the tradition in 2015, pivoting much of Rolling Rock’s production to steel tanks — though it still maintained the glass-lined tanks for its canned beers.

  4. … that inspired another motto embossed onto every bottle.

    The longstanding tradition of the glass-lined tanks is also featured in a pledge printed on every bottle. It reads: “Rolling Rock — From the glass lined tanks of Old Latrobe, we tender this premium beer for your enjoyment as a tribute to your good taste. It comes from the mountain springs to you.” (That motto is also 33 words, which is another theory for the meaning behind that ever-elusive number.)

  5. The brand launched a poster series to highlight visual artists.

    Rolling Rock launched a rollout of posters in collaboration with artists in 1998. The collection, titled “Rolling Rock Poster Series,” includes a number of late-’90s and early-2000s designs in a range of styles, including pop art and abstractionism. Many of the “vintage” posters are available for resale today.

  6. Rolling Rock also hosted five alternative rock music festivals.

    From 2000 to 2005, Rolling Rock hosted an annual alternative rock music festival called the Rolling Rock Town Fair. It drew some of the hottest names in early-aughts rock personalities and swarms of energetic fans to Pennsylvania’s Westmoreland Fairgrounds, just 10 miles from the beer’s birthplace in Latrobe. The Red Hot Chili Peppers headlined the inaugural festival with appearances from Moby, Fuel, and other bands. Later years’ performers included Disturbed and Stone Temple Pilots. Each year, it was a sort of mecca for Western Pennsylvania’s angsty teens, who’d bathe themselves in mud before joining the mosh pit.

  7. Rolling Rock shot for the moon in a false advertisement.

    After acquiring the brand in 2006, Anheuser Busch angered Rolling Rock devotees by shifting its production from Pennsylvania to its macrobrewery in Newark, N.J. As a result, sales began to slump, and to win back favor with fans, the brand launched an ad campaign called “Moonvertising.” Rolling Rock claimed on March 21, 2008, it would project its logo onto the moon with a laserbeam. It was a feat they obviously could not accomplish, further disappointing supporters and keeping the brand in the doghouse for some time.

title: World Cup Is Gone. Beer’s Summer Blues Remain. Now What?
summary:
Long before the World Cup first kicked off earlier this summer, Wall Street analysts, industry insiders, and rank-and-file bar owners were already anxiously talking up the potential sales boost it might bring the beleaguered beer business. All those games, all those fans, all those “occasions”… it would have to add up to something, right? But what?

The article World Cup Is Gone. Beer’s Summer Blues Remain. Now What? appeared first on VinePair.
content:
Long before the World Cup first kicked off earlier this summer, Wall Street analysts, industry insiders, and rank-and-file bar owners were already anxiously talking up the potential sales boost it might bring the beleaguered beer business. All those games, all those fans, all those “occasions”… it would have to add up to something, right? But what?

“On-site at the venues, whatever beer volume comes out of there is a gift, it’s a bonus, and whatever occasions people have off-premise, that’s a bonus as well,” said Dave Williams, the president at Bump Williams Consulting, speaking to Hop Take in advance of the World Cup in early June 2026. “So even with all of these concerns or challenges, I still think that this is a tidal wave of found occasions and reasons to celebrate.” It was the industry’s wave to surf, in other words.

Beer marketers had some fun along the way. “One of the most viral stories of the tournament so far is the sheer decimation of Boston’s beer reserves at the hands of Scotland’s fearsomely thirsty ‘Tartan Army,’” I wrote in mid-June. “It’s a funny story, at [Anheuser-Busch InBev’s] expense: ‘The Scottish fans just drank the place dry, and all they had [left] was Bud Light,’ one eyewitness told the local news.” Other brands, including White Claw and Heineken, tried their hand at fast-follow campaigns, with limited success; Boston Beer Company, whose comms team placed this story to begin with, partnered with JetBlue to “fly in” more Boston Lager. This gag sorta just underscored the point that a vanishingly small amount of the beer is actually brewed in Boston, but sure, fine, cute.

But enough with the marketing. What of the sales, man? Ah. The World Cup swell has come and gone, and the tournament’s tide has finally receded to the point we can get a sense for how it affected beer sales. The upshot is: not great, Bob!

Consider ABI. The company reportedly pumped $110 million into a (very boring) global campaign for Michelob Ultra, and likely gobs more across the breadth of its portfolio and around the world. The logic was straightforward for the longtime brewing partner of the Fédération Internationale de Football Association. “The FIFA World Cup is a once-every-four-years opportunity to build the long-term brand equity of our portfolio,” Michel Doukeris, the company’s chief executive, said on its most recent quarterly earnings call in late July.

But as Brewbound first noted, when an analyst on the call asked about the full-year volume lift ABI was projecting from this massive marketing effort, Doukeris put it at around 0.25%. Now, +25 basis points is nothing to scoff at, and the CEO argued that “the benefits of the activation and everything that we have done and seen from the World Cup will extend far beyond the year.” Maybe! But the beer industry is declining at a much faster rate — around 4.5 percent year-to-date, per the latest Beer Institute tax-paid figures — and ABI’s beer volume is, too, at least here in the United States. Its depletions and shipments for the second quarter of 2026, during which about half the World Cup unfolded, were down 1.9 percent and 0.6 percent, respectively. There may be knock-on benefits to… uh… whatever this was that will be more obvious in Q3, though scan data from multi-outlet grocery, mass retail, and convenience stores tracked by the market research firm Circana shows ABI’s American portfolio down 0.7 percent in dollars and 2.3 in volume for the four weeks through July 12, so maybe not. Either way, this is not shaping up to be a major boost for the country’s biggest macrobrewer.

Elsewhere in the industry, World Cup sales snapshots tell a similar story, if not worse. An analysis of category-level sales by Circana’s longtime beverage-alcohol scan-man Scott Scanlon put beer down 2.1 percent in dollars and 3.4 percent in volume year-over-year for the week through July 19 — the final day of the tournament. Those category declines outpaced the previous four weeks, 26 weeks, and year-to-date benchmarks, suggesting that the beer market may have gotten softer as the World Cup went on. “A bit concerned on [the] overall beer trend at just over the 2026 halfway point for the beer category,” Scanlon noted in a July 26 memo. Beer Marketer’s Insights elaborated in its signature unbylined pidgin last week, noting that a soft June performance “[s]uggests industry shed ~3.5 mil bbls vs yr ago thru the 1st half.” (That’s “3.5 million barrels versus a year ago through the first half of 2026,” for those of you who don’t read BMI-ese.) “Disappointing goin’ up against what was thought to be easier comps as industry slipped nearly [five percent] in the first half of 2025 vs 2024.”

Of course, scan data from Circana and its rival provider NIQ can only augur beer’s performance in the off-premise, and the World Cup was, for so many bargoers, an on-premise drinking occasion. The news was better for beer in those channels, according to sales data from BeerBoard, an on-premise analytics platform. Dollars and volume for draft were up 7.1 and 6.46 percent respectively across the firm’s network of on-premise accounts throughout the tournament. Package revenue was up even more for the period — 11.74 percent — but in a sign of the times, volume was up a little bit less at 5.52 percent. The discrepancy may be due to the fact that BeerBoard’s package data includes “beyond beer” products, which tend to command higher price points and deliver disproportionate revenue growth. On a week-by-week basis, sales surged at the very beginning of the tournament, and again as the U.S. men’s team was playing in the knockout round, then tapered off after both events. By the final week of the tournament, dollars and volume were both slightly down (-1 and -3 percent) compared to the same frames in 2025.

Of course, sales data never tell the whole story. It’s possible that the investments that brewers large and small made to align their brands with the World Cup will pay off down the road, like ABI’s Doukeris envisions for his portfolio. You could imagine, for example, craft breweries winning new repeat customers who first visited their taprooms during watch parties. The tournament might have brought drinkers back to sports bars for long enough to remember that they enjoy drinking draft beer, sending them on their way after the final whistle with vows to do it more often. Hell, if you really squint, you could even see Zoomers warming to the concept of beer specials during live sporting events — dare to dream. There’s a glass-half-full take here.

But the more realistic take, at least with the evidence we have in front of us, is that the World Cup has come and gone, and beer wasn’t really able to catch the wave. This is “tuff” — if you’ll indulge a bit more BMI-ese — because spirits products certainly were. Scanlon’s Circana scans show the category up 4.4 and 8.4 percent in dollars and volume year-over-year in the final week of the tournament, “with Cutwater, Surfside, Sun Cruiser contributing exceptional growth to the category offsetting traditional spirits (outside of Tito’s).” No kidding — Cutwater was up around 60 percent in both dollars and volume that final week. That’s what you’re supposed to do against easier comps!

The World Cup was never going to save the American beer industry, being a once-every-four-years event that won’t return to this continent for the foreseeable future. But it probably should have helped more brewers more than it did. Blame bad marketing, high gas prices, tough competition, or all of the above. But with time ticking off the clock on the second half of summer 2026, and the tournament already fading from the zeitgeist, the result is the same. The beer industry’s summer blues roll on.

🤯 Hop-ocalypse Now

Last decade, the explosion of craft beer in/around cities across the country made the segment an easy shorthand punchline for jokes about effete conspicuous-consuming Millennials. The New Yorker even got in on the action in 2014 with a semi-infamous cover sending up the scene at a stereotypical second-wave beer bar. Ah, memories. This stuff wasn’t quite cliche then, but it was getting there. Which is why I had to double-check what year it was earlier this week when New Yorker staffer and emergent Gen X contrarian Jay Caspian Kang mocked the social-media platform Bluesky (on Bluesky, naturally) as a “little pirate ship that looks like a microbrew meet up”. Ah, man… what? Anyway, loved that one essay you published 16 years ago, though!

📈 Ups…

They say “What’s dead may never die” and that apparently applies to Rogue Ales & Spirits’ intellectual property for Dead Guy Ale, which is currently up for auction… The Great American Beer Festival released its pour list for the 2026 event… Athletic Brewing Co. struck a multi-year deal with MetLife Stadium and the hometown New York Giants and New York Jets… Lawson’s Finest Liquids is launching its own non-alcoholic craft beer called Sip’N…

📉 …and downs

Tilray Brands announced plans to cease production at Terrapin Beer Co.’s plant in Athens, which may make you sad but shouldn’t make you surprised… Ohio mid-major Rhinegeist Brewing’s hot new line extension on Cincy Light is, alas, a vodka-based RTD called Cincy Splash… Monster’s beverage-alcohol division saw net sales decline 15.2 percent, oof…

title: Rogue’s Dead Guy Gets New Lease on Life as Bid for Bankrupt Brewery’s IP Reaches $400k
summary:
Rogue’s Dead Guy might get a new lease on life. Roughly nine months after Rogue Ales & Spirits’ parent company Oregon Brewing filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy, companies are vying for Rogue’s intellectual property (IP). U.K.-based digital marketing agency Silver Scope Media Ltd made a $400,000 bid, and the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the District of Oregon is accepting offers through Aug. 21. Competing bids are required to top Silver Scope’s proposal by $40,000. Oregon Brewing estimated the craft beer brand’s IP at $2 million in its valuation of assets, according to Brewbound.

The article Rogue’s Dead Guy Gets New Lease on Life as Bid for Bankrupt Brewery’s IP Reaches $400k appeared first on VinePair.
content:
Rogue’s Dead Guy might get a new lease on life. Roughly nine months after Rogue Ales & Spirits’ parent company Oregon Brewing filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy, companies are vying for Rogue’s intellectual property (IP).

U.K.-based digital marketing agency Silver Scope Media Ltd made a $400,000 bid, and the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the District of Oregon is accepting offers through Aug. 21. Competing bids are required to top Silver Scope’s proposal by $40,000.

Oregon Brewing estimated the craft beer brand’s IP at $2 million in its valuation of assets, according to Brewbound. Rogue’s IP assets include its website domain; all confidential information, including recipes, manufacturing, specifications, and quality control; biological strain and propagation rights of Rogue’s proprietary yeast; social media accounts; and trademarks, including that of its famed “Dead Guy” IPA.

The search for a buyer of the IP comes five months after Rogue’s bankruptcy liquidation auction, which saw a firesale of its tangible assets like unitanks, hoses, and other brewery equipment.

Oregon-based Valley View Winery filed an objection to the parent company’s intent to sell the IP, as it claims it maintains a “perpetual license” for the rights to Rogue’s wine and wine-based beverages. The winery’s filing states that it trademarked Rogue in 1983, though they reached a settlement agreement with Oregon Brewing in 1997 that gave it rights to the brand’s beer products.

Oregon Brewery’s filing for Chapter 7 came as a shock to the craft beer industry. Rogue abruptly shuttered its distillery and taprooms before citing $17 million in debts against roughly $5 million in assets. Former employees fired back at the parent company for giving little notice of the layoffs and violating the Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification Act.

A hearing for the potential sale and any associated objections will take place on Aug. 26.

content:
In the Southern Rhône Valley’s acclaimed Châteauneuf-du-Pape appellation, Château Rayas both epitomizes the region and stands completely separate from the area’s other revered producers. Like its peers, it gets its powerful personality from the sun-drenched and windswept terroir of the Rhône Valley. But in a region famously defined by blends, Rayas differs by focusing solely on Grenache.

It’s this terroir-driven, single-variety style that has made Rayas a standout among Southern Rhône wines. The estate’s vineyard includes three distinct lieu-dits: Le Levant, Le Coeur, and Le Couchant. When blended, the separate sites come together to form Rayas’s elegant, structured style. Family-owned for generations, the winery has never bowed to outside influence or style.

All these factors make Rayas one of the most coveted Châteauneuf-du-Pape wines, not to mention one of the most expensive, with bottles often selling for a four-figure price tag. While it’s hard to find other wineries focused on varietal Grenache in the region, there are great alternatives where Grenache dominates and captures the magic Rayas portrays in its wines — for a much more accessible price. Here are eight bottles to try.

Delas Frères Châteauneuf-du-Pape ‘Haut Pierre’

Although Delas Frères is mostly a Northern Rhône specialist, the winery’s Grenache-forward Châteauneuf-du-Pape stands out as a special bottling in the otherwise Syrah-dominant portfolio. Grenache comes from sandy soils outside the village of Châteauneuf, and is aged for 12 months in large oak barrels before the final blend, then another year in concrete or steel tanks before bottling. It’s a rich and elegant style that carries the alcohol well. On average, only about 10,000 to 12,000 bottles are produced each vintage, which makes the typical $63 price tag a steal.

Elodie Balme Côtes du Rhône Villages Roaix ’Champs Libres’

Balme founded her namesake domaine at just 23 years old, turning fruit from her family’s property that previously went to a co-operative into her own estate. A disciple of biodynamic and organic practices, she works to preserve the old-vine Grenache under her stewardship, some of which is upwards of 70 years old. To her, “Grenache is a good messenger of terroir,” as she put it during a tasting in 2024. She prefers concrete to oak, saying Grenache is sensitive to oak and its impact. This bottle, available for around $24, is a fresh and vibrant expression of Grenache-led wine.

Domaine de Garriguettes Côtes du Rhône Villages Gadagne ‘L’Amista’

Sébastien Clément, the fourth-generation vigneron of this estate, brings new energy and excitement to winemaking and viticulture. Low-intervention, biodynamic, and regenerative farming guide the work in the vineyards and winery. Like the famed Rayas, “L’Amista” is 100 percent Grenache from old vines planted 1954. But unlike Rayas, this varietal red retails for about $30.

Château de Montfaucon Côtes du Rhône ‘La Côte’

In 1995, Rodolphe de Pins purchased and started restoring an 11th century castle in the Lirac appellation. De Pins, who received a degree from UC Davis and worked at Henschke in Australia and Domaine du Vieux Télégraphe in Châteauneuf-du-Pape, also revitalized the vineyards with a focus on organic farming. Montfaucon wines are prized for being a great value, especially given the high quality. The Grenache-based ‘La Côte’ blend, for example, retails for about $20.

Gour de Chaulé Gigondas ‘La Numéro Huit’

Given its proximity to Châteauneuf-du-Pape, Gigondas has long been considered a value-driven alternative appellation to its famous neighbor. However, estates like Gour de Chaulé prove it has a personality all its own. This family property started estate bottling its wines in the 1970s, with Grenache always the focus. This particular bottling, made with 100 percent Grenache, comes from a parcel of 100-year-old, ungrafted vines. With lots of depth and energy, this $72 bottle is an ideal alternative to Rayas.

Domaine du Vieux Télégraphe Châteauneuf-du-Pape ‘La Crau’

The ‘La Crau’ vineyard’s origins date back to 1898 when farmer and winemaker Hippolyte Brunier planted the first vines. Fairly high in elevation and rather barren, the site proved to be ideal for vines. Today, Vieux Télégraphe’s Grenache-forward wines are prized for their long aging capabilities and structure. The signature La Crau cuvée, retailing for about $136, remains a Châteauneuf-du-Pape icon.

Domaine du Pegau Châteauneuf-du-Pape ‘Cuvée Réservée’

Just like Rayas, Pegau is one of Châteauneuf-du-Pape’s most notable wineries, also like Rayas, its top bottle, ‘Da Capo,’ commands high prices. But the estate’s ‘Cuvée Réservée’ provides a snapshot into Pegau’s prowess with Grenache and other Rhône grapes, but for a more approachable $70 price. Rich and opulent, it still maintains a core of freshness.

Domaine de Longue Toque Gigondas Lieu-Dit ‘Les Trois Yeux’

Domaine de Longue Toque is the label for the estate wines from negociant Gabriel Meffre. This organically farmed wine comes from a high-elevation site with limestone soils in Gigondas, and this particular cuvée, retailing for about $88, comprises three vineyard sites. Grenache leads the way in this elegant but concentrated red with notes of red fruits and black olives.

title: We Asked 8 Sommeliers: Which Sancerre Is Actually Worth the Price?
summary:
There is perhaps no white grape in the world of wine as beloved by drinkers or as maligned by sommeliers as Sauvignon Blanc. Decades of commercialization and the pursuit of mass-market appeal have flattened many expressions of the grape and in the process disillusioned wine professionals about its potential. Through it all, however, one region has stayed steadfast in its commitment to Sauvignon Blanc in its purest form and remained a beloved beacon for wine lovers everywhere: Sancerre.

The article We Asked 8 Sommeliers: Which Sancerre Is Actually Worth the Price? appeared first on VinePair.
content:
There is perhaps no white grape in the world of wine as beloved by drinkers or as maligned by sommeliers as Sauvignon Blanc. Decades of commercialization and the pursuit of mass-market appeal have flattened many expressions of the grape and in the process disillusioned wine professionals about its potential. Through it all, however, one region has stayed steadfast in its commitment to Sauvignon Blanc in its purest form and remained a beloved beacon for wine lovers everywhere: Sancerre.

Located on the eastern edge of the Loire Valley, Sancerre is a region dedicated foremost to the cultivation of Sauvignon Blanc, which accounts for 80 percent of the appellation’s plantings. The region’s distinctive terroir — a mix of Kimmeridgian marl, flinty silex, and stony, limestone-rich soils — gives rise to some of the world’s most nuanced and age-worthy expressions of the grape. The result is a wine defined by its bright acidity, rooted in notes of lemon zest, wet stone, and fresh-cut grass.

Over the years, Sancerre’s enduring popularity has steadily driven the prices up — but not every bottle that dons a $50-plus price tag delivers on quality. Increased interest in the region has challenged sommeliers to dig deeper to find bottles that truly deliver on taste. That’s why we asked eight wine professionals to share which bottles are really worth the elevated cost that comes with the “Sancerre” label.

Sancerre wines that are actually worth the price, according to sommeliers:

  • Vincent Gaudry ‘Le Tournebride’ Sancerre 2024
  • Lucien Crochet ‘La Croix du Roy’ Sancerre 2024
  • Domaine Vacheron Guigne-Chèvres Sancerre
  • Vincent Gaudry ‘Mélodie de Vieilles Vignes’
  • Domaine B. Millet Sancerre ‘Le Chemin Blanc’ 2025
  • Gérard Boulay Chavignol Sancerre
  • Francois Cotat ‘Cul de Beaujeu’
  • Gérard Boulay ‘Clos de Beaujeu’
  • Gérard Boulay Sancerre Les Monts Damnes

“The 2024 ‘Le Tournebride’ Sancerre from Vincent Gaudry has been a recent standout. Vincent is legendary for securing the first biodynamic certification in Sancerre as well as intentionally blending grapes from all three of Sancerre’s primary soil types which is a nod to Parisian bistro traditions. The overall mouthfeel is great and its minerality was gentler than we’ve found with other Sancerres. And at around $50 a bottle, it holds up beautifully to a variety of food pairings from our roasted chicken to our croquettes du jour.” —Jennie Kelley, owner, Fond, Dallas

“I like Lucien Crochet, specifically the 2024 Lucien Crochet Sancerre ‘La Croix du Roy.’ It is a really classic representation but leans more herbal and basil rather than green pepper, which makes it versatile with food. Crisp and citrusy — perfect for summer!” —Charlotte Mirzoeff, general manager and beverage director, Arthur, Brooklyn

“When it comes to sheer consumption, I don’t know if there’s a Sancerre I’ve personally enjoyed or poured for guests more than Domaine Vacheron’s Guigne-Chèvres Sancerre Blanc. Produced from the estate’s famed biodynamically farmed Guigne-Chèvres vineyard, this is a wine that remains laser-focused and expressive, vintage after vintage. It’s always a staple in my home collection. The vineyard’s limestone-rich soils impart an unmistakable minerality that gives the wine an energy that dances across the palate, both playful and powerful. Whether enjoyed fresh in its youth or with a few years of bottle age, Guigne-Chèvres never fails to captivate the entire table and remind both new wine lovers and longtime aficionados that the concept of terroir is alive and well. It’s one of those rare white wines that consistently wins over even the most devoted red wine drinkers.” —Marcie Gsteiger-Cox, wine and service director, Passage, Whidbey Island, Wash.

“Vincent Gaudry has farmed biodynamically since the late ’90s, before the practice was embraced in the region. His wines are textural and precise without being scary expensive. They’re saltier and deeper than your average Sancerre. ‘Le Tournebride’ offers the most easygoing value, but go with ‘Mélodie de Vieilles Vignes’ for something more powerful.” —Grace Rogers, sommelier, Stars, New York City

“For me, Sancerre is a bit of a ‘chef’s night off’ thing, tucked in the back of my wine fridge whenever the need to chill out big time hits. But recently I’ve been really enjoying keeping the wines of Domaine B. Millet on hand with their delicious core of minerality and levity that bucks the flabby Savvy B allegations. Domaine B. Millet Sancerre ‘Le Chemin Blanc’ 2025 is a true standout.” —Alexya Brown, content strategy, Domestique Wine and founder, Vino Verité, Washington, D.C.

“Gérard Boulay, located in the Chavignol sub-zone, is a producer I always look to for cost-to-value Sancerre. Chavignol is the 90210 of Sancerre, containing some of the most coveted single vineyards there. Boulay’s style is very regal and to me, it leans vibrant and textured on the palate, yet remains very taut. You get the herbaceousness and zestiness associated with Sauvignon Blanc, but there is a more mineral, powdery, stony mouthfeel that’s very unique and special.” —Nader Asgari-Tari, director of wine, BCB3 Hospitality, Boston

“Sauvignon Blanc is kind of my comfort grape and I love to see it transmute into all of its various forms. And to me, Sancerre is another one of its gorgeous identities. Francois Cotat ‘Cul de Beaujeu’ offers this tense, generous expression, that I feel blows the door off the style in a freaky, expectation-defying way.” —Hannah Carroll, beverage director, Shy Bird, Boston

“To find Sancerres that are worth the money, I always avoid those in the $30 to $45 range, as those tend to be bottles that were $25 in 2020 and haven’t necessarily gained in quality but certainly have in price. I’d actually pick something higher end like Gerard Boulay’s ‘Clos de Beaujeu.’ It’s a bolder style from some of the best vineyard sites in the region that pairs really well with food. His ‘Monts Damnes,’ while more expensive, is my absolute favorite Sancerre — just incredibly balanced and a really great representation of the region from super steep slopes.” —Savannah Johnson, general manager, Rude Mouth, Brooklyn

title: 7 of the Best Chardonnays From France’s Beaujolais, a Region Famous for Reds
summary:
While the Beaujolais region of France, just south of Burgundy, is famous for its red wines made from the Gamay variety, did you know that it grows small amounts of Chardonnay as well? It turns out that Beaujolais Blanc is one of the best-kept secrets of the broader Burgundy region and is gaining more recognition.

The article 7 of the Best Chardonnays From France’s Beaujolais, a Region Famous for Reds appeared first on VinePair.
content:
While the Beaujolais region of France, just south of Burgundy, is famous for its red wines made from the Gamay variety, did you know that it grows small amounts of Chardonnay as well?

It turns out that Beaujolais Blanc is one of the best-kept secrets of the broader Burgundy region and is gaining more recognition. (Beaujolais is technically part of Burgundy, though the soils and the red wines — Gamay versus Pinot Noir — are distinct, which is why most people in the wine world consider them separate regions.)

The white wines have always intrigued me, and they are quite similar to Burgundian Chardonnays, though perhaps more on the fruity side and made either with or without oak aging. When wood is used, it tends to accent rather than dominate.

Perhaps the biggest difference is the price: While good white Burgundies, even those from the more humble Mâcon subregion in the south, can cost $30, $40, $50, and more, most Beaujolais Blancs are in the more comfortable $20 to $30 range. And well worth it.

Field Blend Selections, the importer of the excellent Domaine Emmanuel Fellot Beaujolais Blanc, notes on its website that only 3 percent of Beaujolais’ vineyards are planted to Chardonnay, adding that “this may be the natural limit since the clay-limestone alluvial soils more suited to Chardonnay are quite rare compared to the Gamay-friendly granite soils.”

Unlike the Gamay-based wines of Beaujolais, many of which are named after the 10 crus in the north of the region, most of the white wines are produced in the south and must be labeled “Beaujolais” or “Beaujolais-Villages.”

Some of the Chardonnays are also labeled “Pierres Dorées,” which means “golden stones” and is named for an area in the south of Beaujolais where the dominant soil is yellow limestone, which is also found in Burgundy. They are considered some of the best Beaujolais Blancs.

With their modest prices and refreshing, easy-to-drink character, Beaujolais Blancs are great wines for informal, late-summer lunches and dinners and for drinking on their own.

Here are seven of the best Beaujolais Blancs:

Jean-Paul Brun Beaujolais Blanc ‘Terres Dorées’ 2024

A delicate, chalky minerality underlies this gorgeous Chardonnay and its notes of pear, honeysuckle, herb-tinged mandarin, and a hint of fennel seed. Jean-Paul Brun farms organically and the wine is aged in steel and concrete tanks. A few retailers sell it for the almost unbelievable price of around $20.

Price: $22
Buy This Wine

Emmanuel Fellot Beaujolais Blanc 2025

This is a wonderful, mineral-driven Chardonnay. Though young, its ripe fruit notes — crisp white peach, citrus, and a touch of honey — make it a pleasure to enjoy right now. There’s a touch of green apple skin, white flowers, and firm acidity on the long finish. Clean, crisp, balanced, and delicious.

Price: $24
Buy This Wine

Georges Descombes Beaujolais Blanc 2023

This wine is only available in magnums, but the double-sized bottle will be a hit when you pour it for your guests or bring it to dinner. Aged in fiberglass tanks and barrels, it’s complex and subtle — the fruit, the minerality, the acidity all in balance. Notes of ripe pear, mandarin, and touches of vanilla, white pepper, and almond combine in this notable Chardonnay.

Price: $63 (1.5 liters)
Buy This Wine

Château Pougelon Beaujolais Blanc ‘Pierres Dorées’ 2024

The aromas transport you to a peach or apricot orchard in late summer, and the ripe stone fruit notes continue in the mouth along with green apple and touches of flint and white pepper. There’s a textured minerality on the long finish. The wine is aged in stainless steel and concrete and sets a benchmark in the region for non-oaked Chardonnay.

Price: $33
Buy This Wine

Domaine de Fa Beaujolais-Villages ‘Leynes Les Magnons’ 2023

Aged in stainless steel tanks and larger used oak barrels, this wine is on the richer side, with hints of vanilla and caramel infusing notes of pear and apricot. It’s also quite herbal, adding another layer of complexity. The owners and winemakers, Maxime and Antoine Graillot, use organic and biodynamic methods and were famous in the Northern Rhône when they expanded to Beaujolais in 2013.

Price: $23
Buy This Wine

Château des Jacques Beaujolais Blanc 2024

This wine reminded me of a Mâcon-Villages Chardonnay from southern Burgundy. It’s fresh, fruity, and uncomplicated with notes of apple, white peach, and hints of honey and orange. A good-value Chardonnay from the north of Beaujolais not far from Pouilly-Fuissé in the Mâcon. Château des Jacques is part of the Louis Jadot Burgundy house.

Price: $24
Buy This Wine

Arnaud Combier ‘Blanc-Sain’ Vin de France Chardonnay 2023

It’s not clear whether this wine is from Beaujolais, Burgundy, or perhaps both. But what I do know is that it’s an excellent Chardonnay. It’s labeled as a Vin de France, which suggests a hybrid origin, and Arnaud Combier produces wines in both regions. In any event, this one drinks way above its price tag with concentrated fruit notes of ripe peach, sweet apple, pineapple, and tangerine, along with balanced acidity and touches of mint, minerals, and caramel. It’s aged in both oak barrels and stainless steel tanks. Alcohol is just 12.5 percent.

Price: $19
Buy This Wine
